utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Have the accused brought in, please. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Good morning to the interpreters. We will now continue hearing the testimony of the Defence witness. Mr. Dubuisson, would you have the witness brought in, please? Have Father Pervan brought in. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Father Pervan, do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. We're going to continue the direct-examination conducted by Mr. Nobilo, and Mr. Hayman who have called you to testify in this case. Mr. Nobilo, please, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Good morning, Father Ivan. Just put that away so we can see each other. Right. So the first subject I would like to deal with this morning is the work of Caritas. Please tell the Court what is Caritas, what kind of an organisation is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, first of all, I have to say a few words by way of introduction. Through the 700 years of the activity of my community, the Franciscans, in Bosnia, it is well-known that the friars took care of the poor, and all who were imperilled in any way. It is also a well-known fact that friars, priests, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, throughout their activity, opened schools, taught children and helped gifted children to get an education in Italy, France and, notably, Austro-Hungary. None of us friars knows how far back the bread of St. Ante dates back to. The bread of St. Ante is our internal Franciscan humanitarian organisation, which takes care of the poor and all those who are needy in any way. Our organisation works in all Franciscan communities. At the level of the general church, there is also care for the poor and the sick, and there is a humanitarian organisation at the level of the entire church which is called Caritas. There are separate organisations in different States where there are several diocese, so there are several Caritas, so to speak. There are several Caritas for example, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, of the Bishop's conference in Bosnia-Herzegovina, which consisted of the Archbishop of Sarajevo, the Bishop of Banja Luka and Trevinsko (phoen) Matrinska in Mostar. Kiseljak directly belongs to Caritas of the diocese in Sarajevo. In 1992, in addition to the humanitarian organisation that existed in the parish of Kiseljak, which is a Franciscan parish, under the instructions of Vinko Pulic, Caritas was established at the level of the parish of Kiseljak within the Sarajevo diocese.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What was your post in the Caritas of the parish of Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the Caritas of the Kiseljak parish I was director of the municipal Caritas.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What was the first activity you carried out, and on what occasion and who did you give this aid to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As soon as we established Caritas at the level of Kiseljak, this was in 1992 in Croatia, war had already broken out, especially in the eastern part of Croatia, notably in Dalmatia. In the parish of Kiseljak, we were collecting aid, and sending it to those who needed it, especially Dubrovnik, Zadar and Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell me, when Sarajevo was laid siege to by the army of Republika Srpska and when it was attacked, who did you personally send trade to inter alia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, we should say that Kiseljak was cut off from Sarajevo. However, as we agreed with the Serbian humanitarian organisation Preporod Renasance, and they made a deal with their army, so from Kiseljak we could send aid to Sarajevo but we had to give 30 per cent of that to Preporod. Of course, there were problems involved. We had to hide certain parcels because the Serb soldiers searched the packages, and if they would often find a name -- find a package with a Muslim name and surname, they would take those parcels away. We would send aid to Sarajevo, and Mr. Ivo Komsic helped the work of Caritas. He later become the President of Bosnia-Herzegovina. With his initiative, with my approval, and I did this very gladly, we sent communications to Jerko Doko, Mr. Alija Itzebegovic and Stefan Kljuic. Of course, we had to conceal all of this because the Serb soldiers would have taken all this away. So we changed their names. Instead of "Alija" we put "Ilija", and we called him Fra Ilija, and Fra Jerko and Fra Stefan, so we used the pseudonyms, calling them friars, and those people in Sarajevo who were seeing this knew exactly who it was for. Perhaps this was not a nice thing to do, but those packages worked much better than those received by other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The war is on in Sarajevo, people are fleeing Sarajevo. Kiseljak is very close to Sarajevo. There are many refugees coming in from Sarajevo. Has Caritas taken part in putting up these refugees, and what nationality did they belong to and what was going on, generally speaking?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A particularly big wave of refugees from Sarajevo came from April 1992 until the end of June 1992. That is to say, within those three months. Most of the refugees got out of Sarajevo by way of Kiseljak, because Kiseljak was not under blockade then. We had buses, so those who wanted to continue managed to do so from here. However, most refugees stayed in Kiseljak. Of course, we did take part in putting up these refugees, but not only Caritas but the entire population did. From Kubilica (phoen) to Kiseljak, this is a 10 kilometre distance. Many people got out of their homes and took out food, cakes, drinks, clothes and offered all of this to the refugees. Some people were even brought in dead. At a checkpoint in Kubilica a lady had a heart attack. A lot of people say that this was because she was afraid and others say that she was very happy to get out of the hell of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Please tell the Court whether all these refugees belonged to the same ethnic group or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. The -- the least number of refugees were Serbs, and the most were Croats or Muslims. So if I were to speak of my own estimate, I would think it was a 50/50 ratio.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. In the second half of 1992, you -- or rather, Caritas organised a collection centre, a warehouse of sorts; wasn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Since in Split we had a collection centre and a warehouse in Split, and before that, actually, we had one which was in Sarajevo, so we would bring food in to Kiseljak so it would be closer to the other Caritas, Tuzla, Kiseljak, Zenica, Zepce, Kresevo, Fojnica, Busovaca. And initially, our upper church was our warehouse. You don't know this, but the church in Kiseljak consists of two parts. It has a crypt and the upper part of the church was not being used, it's a very big area, and that's where we kept all this food and distributed it throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina, or, rather, those centres that were accessible at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In Kiseljak you were not the only humanitarian organisation. There was also Merhamet and the Red Cross. Can you tell us about these other organisations, whether there was co-operation between them and who covered which area of work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The municipality of Kiseljak, before the war, had a population consisting of two ethnic groups primarily before the war; 53 per cent were Croats, 46 per cent were Muslims, 3 percent Serbs, and the remaining 1 per cent were those who were uncommitted or who chose to be Yugoslavs. They called themselves Yugoslavs. As the war broke out in Bosnia-Herzegovina, quite openly, notably in Sarajevo and in Posavina and around Krajina around Banja Luka, we established Caritas, but the Islamic community also established a humanitarian society called Merhamet. At the level of the municipality, the civilian authorities had an international organisation, the Red Cross. In 1992, to the great satisfaction of all Caritas, Merhamet and the Red Cross worked together. When I say that they worked together, I mean the following: We agreed that Caritas would take over care for the Catholics, for the Croats, that Merhamet would take care of the Muslims, and that the Red Cross would coordinate the work of these two societies. We reached such an agreement and this functioned very well. Caritas and Merhamet were supposed to compliment each other, so what Caritas did not have we would get for free from Merhamet, and what Merhamet did not have they could get from Caritas for free. We gave each other as much as was needed if this was possible, of course, if we had the required amounts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell me, when did Merhamet stop working on the territory of the municipality of the Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Merhamet worked in 1992, and then they had some internal problems of their own in their organisation. They did not agree with the leadership of Merhamet, so, therefore, they had less and less food. And also, the donations they were receiving became smaller and smaller. Merhamet worked in 1992, and in 1993. I do not know why and how they no longer functioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Does that mean that at one point in time you started taking care of the Muslim population too that needed assistance? If that is so, could you please explain to the Court which villages you brought aid to, or, rather, the Muslim populations of those villages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Before Merhamet stopped working, many Muslims came to the church, because that's where the warehouse was, and they asked me personally to give them food. During this first period of time I would tell them to go to Merhamet, and they said, "There's nothing down there, we want to get supplies from you." Of course, at the time when Merhamet was working as well, I did give aid to the Muslims, and often it was easier for me to give something to a Muslim than to try to justify myself and to make excuses because of the agreement reached between Merhamet and Caritas. However, since Merhamet worked less and less, more and more Muslims came to us, to Caritas, and received aid there. At that time, we gave the most assistance to those Muslims who were closest to the church. That is to say, Muslims in town, Muslims in Rotilj, Muslims in Visnjica, but other villages where they worked, but also at like Duhreta (phoen), Polje, Radanovici, Grahovcici, Han Ploca, Palez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When you say "town" are you referring to the town of Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: At one point in time when you reached your peak, how many people were you feeding, Caritas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean at the peak or at any time?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: No, I'm saying what was the maximum number of people that received aid and food from Caritas, refugees or the local population, irrespective of ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were 18,000.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell me, did you have any problems? We know, from this trial and otherwise, that in Bosnia there were interethnic tensions and later conflicts. Were you under pressure of any kind because you gave help and aid to the Muslims and you are a Catholic organisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I shall tell you the following: Before the conflict with the Muslims, that is to say between the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the HVO, in the entire municipality, throughout the public, everyone knew that the priest from Caritas is giving aid to the Muslims. Many knew this, many saw this. None of the official authorities, military, civilian and political objected to this. They didn't ask me why I was doing this. Of course, there were some people, especially during the war, who were affected by the war, who lost their nearest and dearest. There were people who were wounded, people who were expelled and who were muttering complaints as to why aid was being given to those who had expelled them. You'll have to understand this. At that time, per week, I would have 10 or 15 funerals for people who got killed. So there were families, there were children, there were old parents, so there were such objections that were raised by some people. Not that often to me personally but there were rumours. People talked throughout town, in their homes, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell me -- at this point we're just talking about Caritas -- in relation to your humanitarian work, did you have any contact or conversation with Tihomir Blaskic exclusively related to helping Muslims through Caritas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In 1992, through the period from the spring until the winter, I was in contact many times with Mr. Blaskic. At that time we did not specifically talk about Caritas, but he knew what I was doing. He knew that I was distributing aid to the Muslims as well. He was in Kiseljak when we took in Muslims from other places too, and I did have a conversation with him about Caritas as well. This was in the second half of the month of May 1993. This was at the funeral of Mato Lucic. In Kiseljak he's called Maturice. This was a tête-à-tête conversation, although they were surrounded by other people. We exchanged a few words, he asked me how I was, what I was doing, what I knew, whether there were any problems, and I said that I was sad, and dismayed and tired, and that Caritas would eat me up, I said. I also told him that there would be problems probably with people, Muslims, who remained in Kiseljak. They didn't have an organisation of their own, and that they would come to seek aid from Caritas in the municipality of Kiseljak. And he said the following: "You are a priest. You are a Franciscan. You are a Friar. You know what your calling is. It means the following: You have to give."

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell me, were people revolted when Maturice was killed and can you tell me a few words about the reputation he enjoyed amongst the Croats? Was mention made of this that there would be additional problems in this respect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Anto Lucic Maturice was a young man whom I have known since 1983, because I was in Capelan his native parish, the parish of Bembrdo, and he was enrolled at the Yugoslav People's Army military school and had to be a party member, which means that publicly he was not able to declare his religion. He was not able to christen his children and have his wedding rights performed in a church. I knew that and when I was a priest in my younger days, secretly we would hear his confession and give him absolution. When the war broke out, as an officer of the Yugoslav People's army, he came to Kiseljak black, he was a young man who always found time to smile, he would joke, he was a very clean man, kept himself clean, he was dark featured and in the army he was highly respected. The army liked him. He was the deputy of the head of the barracks in Kiseljak. That is to say, the head of the military units in Kiseljak. He was killed, I think, on the 10th of May when there was a cease-fire of some sort, and when we had hopes that the war would perhaps not break out and that those who make such decisions would be able to come to a decision. But he died and was killed during a reconnoitring activity. There were two other soldiers with him when he was killed. There was an enormous funeral with many people attending. There was the army, there were soldiers who came to the funeral, and they got drunk out of desperation. People who were revolted by everything that had happened, and they said, "Well, they've skilled our best man."

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And in circumstances of this kind, you found the need to talk to Blaskic about aid and assistance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was the motive for my talks with Blaskic, because as you know, I too am only a man and I have my own fears.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And before we move into another area, the refugees to the municipality of Kiseljak, I would like to ask the registrar to give us the number of the exhibit for the series of documents which represent lists that Caritas drew up and referred to aid and assistance to the Muslims in Muslim villages.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D424/1 through 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Would you pass the documents around, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It was D423.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the documents to be handed out, would you please leaf through the documents, and then we will discuss them. Father Ivan, please tell us how I came by those documents. Who gave me the documents, and are the photocopies authentic representations of the documents you gave me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they are authentic copies of the originals that I have in my possession.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell me, please, what does this set of documents, this set of lists represent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This set of lists represents the names and surnames of individuals who received aid from Caritas, and are of the Muslim ethnic group and of the Islamic religion. I should also like to add one sentence here, and that is that in Caritas we did not have a column for ethnic group, nationality; but here it is easy to see from the names and surnames who belongs to which ethnic group.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. We're now going to move to another subject, and it is refugees in the Kiseljak municipality. Do you know how many Catholics your parish had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. My parish, before the war, had 4.300 Catholics living in it, and mostly Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell me, in 1992, where did the refugees come to, from which areas, and what ethnic group did they belong to and who were they fleeing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In 1992, up until the month of June, we had an influx of refugees, mostly from Sarajevo and the environs of Sarajevo, and from places which had already been taken control of by the Serbian army. Among those refugees, mostly there were Croats and Muslims, and some Serbs from mixed marriages who had mixed marriages. From June onwards, we had an influx of refugees, mostly from the Banja Luka region, from the Travnik area, from Zenica, Konjic and the environs. That is say all Rakovica, that is to say all the places which had been taken control of by the Serbian army. That is, I'm talking about the year 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How many refugees did you take in at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that in September, already, the number of refugees who had decided to remain in Kiseljak, in the parish of Kiseljak, was at least 1.500.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Up until the end of that year, there were a little more than 2.000 refugees, in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So, these 2.000 refugees, for the most part, had fled in the face of the Serb onslaught. What happened in January of 1993? Did you have a new wave of refugees? Where did they come from, and who did they flee from, and what ethnic group did they belong to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In January, 1993 there was an attack between the BH army and the HVO, and this was in the region of the Kiseljak municipality, that is to say, between Kiseljak municipality and the Busovaca municipality. This conflict took place in the village of Bilalovac, Kacuni, Oseliste, Bukovice, Gusti Grab, Pezici, Nezirovici and Donja Polje. At that time, in that conflict, the HVO lost the battle, and there were a large number of refugees, approximately 2.000 of them. They fled from Kiseljak, they fled from the war, and according to their ethnic group, they were Croats, and they came from the villages of Bilalovac, Kacuni, Bukovice, Poselisje, Gusti Grab, and from all the villages, the northern lying villages of the Brestoska parish. And as I said, there were about 2.000 of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Those 2.000 Croats who had fled in the face of the war, and the villages that you enumerated, we're not going to show them on the map now, but they are located between Bilalovac and Kacuni, that is to say, they are partially from the Busovaca municipality and in part from the Kiseljak municipality; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, Bilalovac, up to Klokops (phoen) and including Klokope (phoen), belongs to the Kiseljak municipality, Poselisje, Gusti Grab, Bukovci, Nezirovici, Donja Polje belong to the Busovaca municipality. So the conflict was between the army of BH and the HVO, and it occurred on the borderline between the two municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So after this second wave of refugees, Croats who had fled from Kacuni and Bilalovac, up until the month of April, there were no new waves of refugees. But before we go on to discuss the month of April, I should like to suggest that we read a report from Catholic clergy from Bosnia, which you, yourself, signed and which, according to our knowledge, was written at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I should now like to ask this document to be handed out. I apologise, the Croatian original exists in one sample only, and I'm going to have it Xeroxed during the break, and we shall be submitting a translation of it. As it exists in English, I'm going to read it out so that it can be translated into French.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D424, for the BCS version, and 424A for the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I am going to read the text, the interpreters do not have the text in English. It is titled "Statement by the Catholic clergy from Central Bosnia." "For 13 years of permanent presence and tradition, and out of the feeling of responsibility for our people, and before our people, gives us the right and makes it incumbent upon us to raise our voice. We feel it to be our duty to draw attention to both the Croatian and Muslim people that we condemn the tragic events which have happened in this region against the will of both peoples. Without intending to create policy or to decide upon any political system or alliance, we support the basic rights of every man living in this region, which is sacred to us. Immorality and crime do not bring any good to those who commit them, let alone to those who are subjected to them. The tradition of this unique region and people, especially of the Croatian people and its customs, is to respect every man and his freedoms, and to live in the spirit of tolerance and Christian love with all the people with whom we share the space, the spirit and the breath. Therefore, we demand that those persons in authority, either civilian or military, and all those who," in adverted commas, "in the name of the people, commit any acts which are contrary to those, and sow the seeds of fear and hatred should be isolated and uncovered in the name of the basic right of a life of freedom to every man. We recommend that truthful people from both sides, who enjoy the reputation and trust, found joint commissions which will visit our whole region and restore the confidence which has been seriously shaken. In an effort to stop all unwanted events, we call God's blessing and wish peace and good will to all those who can hear this voice of protest, as well as to those who think differently." And this document is signed by a number of fathers, first of all, we have Father Likica Malicovic (phoen), the guardian of Fojnica, and Father Ivan Pervan, the parish priest of Kiseljak. So, tell us, please, first of all, whether you gave us this statement, this proclamation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And tell us the circumstances under which it came into being, why it was written, and in which way you published it and made it public to the people.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was written out of the need that was felt at the time, which was not a good time, that it be the voice of reason, that it be the voice of human dignity, and that it be the voice of believers and those people who believe in God and who wish all people to be brothers. It was written at the time before the April conflicts. We compiled this document, wrote it, signed and published it in the public information media via the local radio stations, local television, but also via the media which did not only exist in Kiseljak, but elsewhere, as well. So this was published by the Slobodna Dalmacija newspaper in Split, as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: However, in April a new wave of refugees broke out in your parish. Can you explain to the Court -- and before that, may we place a map on the ELMO, and I should like to ask you to try and find the villages from which the new wave of refugees came to the Kiseljak municipality.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The map is D425.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: On the ELMO, please. Would you place the map on the ELMO, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: We will move on to a larger map, because what I wanted to show you does not exist on this map. Would you please tell the Trial Chamber where the refugees came from in April, 1993 in the Kiseljak municipality, from which villages, and how many of them were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In April, 1993, refugees came from the northern villages of the Brestoska parish, what remained of them, and especially from the southern part of the Kiseljak municipality, the part which links up the region towards Sarajevo. They are the villages of Pirin, Bukovica Mokrine, Zabrdje, Medvjedice, Fojakovac (phoen), and then we have from Potofzezo (phoen), and refugees which were able from Zupa to come to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Would you please point Kiseljak out on the map to us, and then the area from which the refugees came in from the villages that you enumerated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So that is the town of Kiseljak and the centre of your parish. Where did the refugees come from?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Usher, would you please give the witness the microphone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From Gunjaca (phoen) and Brestoska, the houses which were near the church. And from the churches, the delineation line and the frontline was 100 metres away from the church. I'm going to show you Pirin and the other places, but they won't be able to hear me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: We have a new microphone now, so you will be able to be heard.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bukovica, Mokrine, Zezelovo, Zabrdje, Medvjedice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell me, what area of the municipalities, was it south-west?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is the southern reaches of the municipality, that is to say, the part of the municipality linking up the territory towards Sarajevo, south of Kiseljak, the road towards Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, you may take your seat again. And tell the Court, please, what ethnic group did these refugees belong to from the villages that you have just enumerated and indicated to us, and who were they fleeing from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All the refugees were of the Croat ethnic group, Zupa and Kiseljak, about 1.500 of them came. Some of them remained in Zupa, Lepenaca, Bambrdo and some went to Zupa Gromiljak, to the parish of Gromiljak, and they fled in the face of the BH army. So, it was the Muslim army that they were fleeing from.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The new wave of refugees came in July, 1993. Can you explain to the Court the municipalities that these refugees had fled from, how many of them there were, what ethnic group they belonged to and who they were fleeing from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In July, on the 3rd and 4th of July, 1993, a large number of refugees, about 2.500 of them, came to the Kiseljak parish from the Fojnica municipality and from the Kresevo municipality. From the Kresevo municipality the Dezevice parish, and from the Fojnica municipality from Fojnica proper, and all the upper villages around Fojnica, that is to say, the villages linking up the area towards Gornji Vakuf, Sebesic and the Laska Ravan. They had also fled after the conflict between the BH army and the HVO because their houses were set fire to, there were a lot of dead there, and they were all Croats, those who came to Kiseljak. And amongst them there was a priest who was in the village, he was not able to go back to Fojnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The next large wave of refugees came in November, 1993. Can you explain again to the Court which municipalities and which places these refugees came from, how many of them were there, what ethnic group did they belong to and why did they run away?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Today is exactly five years from the date on which this took place. Exactly five years ago today, around 3.500 refugees came to Kiseljak. These are refugees who came from Catici, Kakanj, all the villages of Kraljeva Sutjeska, I can enumerate all of them if necessary, from Zupa, Borovica, from upper and lower Borovica, from Vares and all the surrounding villages. They came after the conflict between the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the HVO. Through Brgul they came to Kiseljak. In Kiseljak, later, 2.500 of them stayed on, but I also know for sure that many of these refugees immediately continued towards Stolac and Capljina, where they live until the present day. So, 3.500 of them came to Kiseljak, 2.500 stayed on for good, and the other refugees from Kakanj proceeded to Herzegovina where they live until the present day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell me, let us concentrate, rather, on state municipalities, rather than parishes. Is it true that in 1993, in November, these refugees were from Vares and Kakanj, those municipalities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You told us what parishes these refugees came from; but if we were to look at municipalities, the state government units of administration, would it be correct to say that these refugees in November, 1993 came from the municipality of Vares and the municipality of Kakanj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the municipality of Kakanj and the municipality of Vares.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that before the war your parish had 4.300 Catholics.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: During the war, did the number of your parish go down? I mean amongst the original population.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, during the war I had less than 3.500 of them. From 1991 to 1993, many of them went to safer places, especially to western Europe, and during the war in 1993, I never had more than 3.500 parishioners.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So, in your municipality, or rather, in your parish, where there are less people, which is smaller than the municipality of Kiseljak, how many people did you receive at your peak time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can prove and show that at end of 1993, in my parish, there were 14.000 refugees. But we must bear in mind the following: Kiseljak does not have only one parish, it also has the parish of Lepenica and the Zupa Gomoljica and of Lepenez (phoen). Gromoljan also took a lot of refugees, and at one point it was assumed that in the municipality of Kiseljak there were over 30.000 refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So, if we are now to dwell on your parish only, which you know the best, of course, there were 3.500 Catholics from amongst the local population, the original population, you received 14.000 people on the territory of your parish, all of them Catholics, Croats. This large concentration of refugees, which considerably exceeded the possibilities you had for feeding them, giving them shelter, et cetera; did this also have a destructive effect on interhuman relations, interethnic relations, in particular?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, it was terrible. There is one more thing I wish to add. When the refugees came in, or rather before the war, Kiseljak and the municipality had 25.000 inhabitants. During the war the municipality lost a lot of its territory, and therefore, a lot of the housing facilities. Also during the war many houses were destroyed, mined, torched, and when the refugees came in, although they are Catholics and Croats, and although they were often relatives, they quarrelled and especially over housing space, and this certainly had an effect on interethnic relations in the parish and in Kiseljak in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The parish of Kiseljak and the municipality of Kiseljak was abandoned by a large number of Muslims. Can you explain to the Court under which conditions this happened? What were the reasons why the Muslims were leaving the municipality of Kiseljak and your parish, for instance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina it was the same. When the army would lose a battle somewhere, the army would withdraw, and together with the army the people would leave, too. This happened with all three armies, with all three peoples, this happened wherever there were conflicts, wherever there was war. The other reason was, a very important one, was the following: I shall give you an example, rather. When the refugees from Fojnica came in, they went to the Muslim village of Duhre, and they told the villagers, Muslims of Duhre, that your Muslims had evicted them, our houses are in Fojnica, you go to Fojnica and we will live here, and that's exactly what happened. Later on in peacetime, until the present day, many houses are occupied in this way, people reached that kind of agreement, you live in my house and I will live in yours. There were quite a few such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was it always a matter of agreement, as you mentioned, between the population of Fojnica and the population of Duhre, or was there violence, too, and were some Muslims evicted from their houses by force by some of the refugees, and also by some of the extremists from amongst the Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were forceful evictions of Muslims from their homes. There were extremists in the Croatian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: As time went by, the village of Rotilj became the home of a large number of Muslims. Tell the Court more about the village of Rotilj. Who lived there predominantly, what were the characteristics of this village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The village of Rotilj is a village that adjoins the town of Kiseljak. Most of the population was Muslim. The houses belonged to Croats and Muslims, but then the Croat village of Bjorne (phoen) is adjacent. They are only about 50 to 100 metres away, so these are Croat houses. This is a village that is by an asphalt road, it is a village that had electricity, telephones, a village that had a water supply of its own, its own fields, and it also had direct access to the forest. Many of the villagers worked in Kiseljak. So, it was one of the bigger Muslim villages. They could work in agriculture and work in the city at the same time, and also sell timber, which is very important, because 70 per cent of the population of Kiseljak still uses wood for heating.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: During 1993, during the April fighting, a large number of Muslims from other villages came to the village of Rotilj so they could live there. Tell me, why were these villagers, these Muslims, fleeing their villages? These were not villagers who fled together with the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, so what are the other reasons that compelled these people to move into Rotilj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The fighting between the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Croatian Defence Council started in Rotilj during the first days of the conflict, and this conflict was one of the first to end, as well, because the HVO won the battle in Rotilj, took away the arms, and peace came to prevail there. After the first fighting in Rotilj, there were never more conflicts, there were never anymore conflicts. A few houses were burned down in Rotilj, however, many houses remained intact. Many Muslims who were evicted by the refugees thought that the fighting would stop, perhaps, and they wanted to be closer to their own homes, and they went to Rotilj, either to stay with their relatives or in an abandoned house. I remember an example of this kind, a man from Kiseljak, Mirsad Mujkic, he was a baker, and at that time I was not in Kiseljak, he was evicted from his own home, together with his wife and two children, and a family came to stay there, a family of nine. He also went to Rotilj with his wife and children. When I came home, after my trip, I brought him into the house of Zdravko Lukic (phoen), a Croat in town, and that is where he spent the war, together with his family. They are Muslims, but they spent the war in the house of Zdravko Lukic, and the civilian and military and political authorities knew about this. So, many people went to Rotilj simply trying to get away from the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell me, who are the Muslims who came to Rotilj, from what villages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge from Duhra Ardanovic, Duhre, Pernjaci (phoen), Palez, Kacuprija (phoen), Donji Palez, Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You described the forceful eviction of people by refugees and Muslim villages and in the town of Kiseljak through the example that you just mentioned to us; and tell me, did you know of the HVO, the army coming in to a village, putting people into trucks and moving them out of the village concerned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not aware of such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In Rotilj, a ramp was placed at the entrance to the village; who put this there and why, and for what reason, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When the fighting stopped in Rotilj itself, when the fighting stopped in Rotilj itself, then at the entrance into the village, just above town, a ramp was placed. It was simply a log which would be moved by hand up and down.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Just a minute. I think that there is a mistake in translation. When we are talking about a ramp, we are talking about a BRKLJA, and in English it was said "ramp", and I think that that means some kind of a take off. Could you please describe what was on the road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let us assume that there is a road between me and the Honourable Judges, and let us assume it is 20 centimetres wide, and then the ramp I'm referring to is a log that was placed as a road block. It is a log, five to ten centimetres wide, 4 to 5 metres long; so, it's there as a road block, rather.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Who else was there and why was this done?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So this roadblock, as we are going to call it from now on, was placed at the initiative of the people from the village of Borina. The reason is the that Muslims from the village of Rotilj wanted to protect themselves from those people who wished to go to Rotilj and to harm the Muslims in some way, either to rob them or to mistreat them spiritually or physically. So that was the main reason. First days, and I remember that well, at that roadblock were two elderly men without any weapons. Their task was the following: If somebody wanted to get into Rotilj, they should use the phone that they had there to let the police or the army know about it. I didn't ask them who they were supposed to notify. This ramp was a precautionary measure so that something wrong wouldn't happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Perhaps now we could distribute the maps that we already introduced into evidence, and we have copies for the Honourable Judges and for our colleagues from the Prosecution. Father Ivan, you can sit down now. We'll bring the ELMO up to you and it will be more practical that way. So if you'll take a seat. Would you repeat the number of the exhibit, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: For the map it's D425.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Sit down, please. I'm going to ask you a question. According to your knowledge -- I'm going to ask you a question. As far as you know, was Rotilj a camp or not, a prison camp or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I maintain that it was not a camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Why do you say that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because the barrier or the roadblock was set up at the entrance to the village of Rotilj in a place called Privori. From the village of Rotilj there are many other roads which can be taken to lead you to all the roads in the Kiseljak municipality, and roads in the Kresevo municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Let us dwell for a moment on these roads, and turn, if you will, to the map, please, and explain to the Court what number 1 marked on the map means, what it denotes, and use your indicator to tell us what number 1 means.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Number 1 is the exact position of the roadblock.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Would you show us the road from Kiseljak to Rotilj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What do the numbers from 2 to 8 represent, and the arrows there, the numbers and the arrows from 2 to 8?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These numbers from 2 to 8 and the arrows represent alternative paths from which you can get out of Rotilj.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can you use a tractor or car to traverse those roads?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you can still exit by car, such as a Volkeswagen Golf, although the roads have not been seen to for the last five years. They have not been repaired for the last five years.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell us whether around the village of Rotilj, which is a circle marked on the map, whether there were any guards, and whether there were any mines, and whether these roads were guarded in any way, the roads around the village.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Around the village of Rotilj, as far as I know, there were no obstacles, no barriers, no guard points, checkpoints, and the road was not mined.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In addition to the roadblock on the road which was made up of a log, as we already said, and two HVO soldiers manning it, could you reach the villages circumventing that block?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but this is the easiest way because it is an asphalt road, whereas in other places, if somebody wanted to go to the village, the villagers, for example, from Borina, that is number 2 on the map, those who wanted to protect these people would see it and they would react to the situation, so that it was the psychological indicator to those who wished to enter that -- the village was being guarded and watched over that nothing terrible could happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Were there any Croat houses and Croatians in the village of Rotilj throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, throughout the war, and before the war, during the war, and after the conflict as well in the village of Rotilj, which is predominantly a Muslim village, there were Croats. Immediately after the roadblock, the barrier, towards Rotilj, there were Croats living there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How many Croatian houses and how many Croats lived in the village of Rotilj throughout 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Up until the arrival of the refugees, the Croat refugees to the village of Rotilj, who still live in Rotilj, together with the Muslim population in Muslim houses there were at least 10 houses which were permanently inhabited in Rotilj. And let me repeat once again, and I'm going to show you the road from Rotilj and Borina, which are asphalt roads, and between those two places Croats and Muslims live along side each other. They live along side each other today, they did so before, during, and as I say, after the conflict. (Indicating). So between these two roads Croats and Muslims lived together, from the roadblock, during the conflict, and Croats used to live here as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell me, please, whether the Muslims from Rotilj would go to your church in Kiseljak on business of any kind.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They used to come. They could go by the roadblock or via Borina and past the cemetery.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could you show us the road they would have used?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They came this way and took what they needed (indicating). I should like to mention that at that time, while the ramp --I'm using the word "ramp", but shall I say the barrier, or obstacle or block, while it existed in Privori and throughout the time after that, these people had a Croat physician in the village. Actually, it was a lady doctor that saw to their health, and they would come to her at all times during the day and night. If they had other requirements, other needs, they would either come to the doctor up to the roadblock, ask for medical aid and assistance. And I know this personally because I visited the lady doctor, and I know that an ambulance, together with a doctor, and a nurse and the driver would go to Rotilj and give medical assistance there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, do you think this is a good time to take a break, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I was waiting for the end of the questions about Rotilj. We're going to suspend the hearing until 11.50

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will now resume. Have the accused brought in, please. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Would I like to apologise for the delay. It was my fault, but I had some other business to attend to during the break, since the break is only the time that I can. However, I am not guilty of the fact that the map has fallen off.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Father Pervan, before the break we talked about the roads leading out of Rotilj. Nobody guarded them, they weren't mined. Could you tell me and then could you show me on the map whether one could go from Rotilj to territory controlled by BH army? If so, could you please show this to us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. One could reach the territory under the control of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in this way, and in several ways, rather. There were many roads leading towards that territory. All these roads went through the forest, but they were all accessible and you could go through them. I'm going to show you at least one road that one could take to -- from Rotilj to the territory controlled by the army of BH. So it went through Suplja Bukva, Jelacke, through Katici and Popina (phoen), and to Rakova Noga, and from Rakova Noga towards Ramici, Hodzici, Handzici, Grmacki and from Grmacki the road to Crnicki Kamenik, which was then and is until the present day under the control of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I'll show you on the big map too.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The map is D426.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is Rotilj. This is the road that goes to Suka Bukve from this side, and it goes back to Jelacke. The same road can be taken the other way around. Underneath Vis again to Ravni Grad and then to Jelacke. From Jelacki the road goes down to Popina one and a half kilometres away, then to Rahmici and Hodzici. I have to take a look so I can see properly. From Hodzici and Grmacki it goes to Crnicki Kamenik. Crnicki Kamenik is a Croatian village with a chapel which was taken by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it stayed there. And this entire territory down here is under control of the BH army, and is so until the present day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, please sit down. Father Pervan, what is the first time you personally went to Rotilj, on what occasion and why?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was at the very beginning when the fighting broke out. The fighting that was less intensive than the conflicts that took place before that, and a lot less intensive than what ensued. Near the church in Kiseljak, and near my flat, there is a hotel called Dalmacija, which was the UNPROFOR base. One evening, at 10.00, Mr. Daniel Furman came from UNPROFOR. I don't know what he did in UNPROFOR, I don't know his exact post, but we often saw each other. Later on, he drove me in a carrier to Fojnica when the priests were killed, and he came and told me that in UNPROFOR they had food for Muslims, notably for children, in Rotilj, but that there was a roadblock up there, and then he asked me to take that food up there. I got ready. I took my own car, I put the seats down, I went to the UNPROFOR base. I loaded the food into the car and everything else that was there, and I drove it to Rotilj between 10.15 and quarter to eleven at night. That is to say, between 10.15 p.m. And 10.45 p.m. I went straight to Salko Hodzic's house. I gave this to him. When I came to Rotilj I walked into the first house where the Muslims were and I asked which one of them was in charge of their affairs, and he -- and they said, "Salko Hodzic." I went to see Salko Hodzic. I gave it to him, and we have been co-operating until the present day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell me, after this first trip you took, in a way we can see from this document that Rotilj became part of your regular system of supplies. After that would you come to Rotilj regularly and bring in food?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not take food to Rotilj any more, I would go there to see them, have coffee and talk to them, but the director of Caritas and the workers of Caritas would invariably take them food.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell me, from your perception and from the conversations you had with other people, did you see anything that would lead you to the conclusion that Rotilj was a camp, or did any one of the Muslims complain to you that they were in a camp and that they were not free?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Rotilj was not a camp. The Muslims in Rotilj did complain of their living conditions. They were complaining because their relatives were not there, there was shooting, people were getting killed, there was a war going on, but in Rotilj no one persecuted them, especially when other Croats came to Rotilj. Then I was often a witness of them drinking coffee together. I assert that Rotilj was not a camp. What all other refugees from other places had, they had too. Of course, we have to say it was not easy for them by virtue of the fact that there was a war between the Croats and Muslims, and they were Muslims. And it was not easy for them from a psychological point of view, and psychological pain is a very difficult thing as well, but I assert once again that Rotilj was not a camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In 1993, when you went to see Muslims and had coffee with them --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In 1993, when you went to Rotilj to have coffee with the Muslims as you said, did somebody say, "This is a camp, we are detained"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No one ever told me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Please tell the Court, why did you take food to Rotilj while other refugees came to the Caritas warehouse to collect food? What was the reason for this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I shall tell you the following: For a long period of time, we would store food in our upper church. The churchyard is big enough for 30 cars only, so it's a very small churchyard, although the church itself is big. We wanted to avoid any kind of commotion. That is why we took food to Rotilj ourselves, for two reasons. And we also took food to Brnjaci for another reason. In Rotilj, where the Muslims were, we took food because it was easier for us to load this food in large quantities and ask them to distribute it themselves. So it was easier for us this way, because the Caritas organisation of Kiseljak had six and a half thousand voluntary days of work. That is to say that very many people worked for years. So we didn't want to have any commotion. That was one reason. The other reason was that, heaven forbid, any kind of incident break out in front of the church or in the church, because the fathers and mothers of people who got killed in Kiseljak in those days were coming to the church, and that is why I took food to Brnjaci, which was a 100 per cent Croat and Catholic village. So those were the reasons why I did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What were supplies like in Rotilj at that time? Did Rotilj have more or less food than Visoko, for example, where Muslims lived under BH army control?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I must say something that was positive in Kiseljak and Visoko. From September and October, at the lines near Kiseljak and Visoko, there were not any attacks when the Croats from Kiseljak and the Muslims from Visoko were manning the lines. Many people from Kiseljak and Visoko knew each other because they are only 13 kilometres away. A lot of them went to Kiseljak and a lot of them went to Visoko, before the war. So, when the BH army was on one side, consisting of people from Visoko, and on the other side when they were Croats from Kiseljak, there was no shooting at these lines. People would shout and talk to one another because the trenches were often 10 or 20 metres away from one another. On one occasion on a radio frequency, they had agreed on what the radio frequency would be, it was 14.500, they talked to one another without introducing themselves. An HVO soldier told the man on the other side, "I know who you are," and he said, "no, you don't," and he said, "I know him, I know you, and I know your father, and I watch him every day from my house. You are Hodzic's men," and he said, "Tell my father to send me a parcel to Visoko." So from that one may conclude that Muslims in Visoko had less food than the Muslims in Kiseljak. I know for sure that a sack of flour in Visoko was a hundred Deutschmark and in Kiseljak no one bought flour, and the Muslims didn't buy flour, either.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: We heard before this Court that Rotilj was overpopulated, that there were a lot of people staying in one house; and how would you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that is true. In Rotilj, as I said, some houses had burned down. So, there was less housing space. A lot of people came to Rotilj, and I know that in the house of Salko Hodzic, there were 17 people staying there. I went there for coffee and it was hot, so we sat outside. But I must say that in my house, also, the parish house, on the floor, on sponge mats, I had 15 people staying there for 15 days, that is where they slept and that is where they ate. When refugees would come in, and when they would seek shelter, then Muslims would go and stay with each other, especially in bigger houses. There is one more thing I wish to mention in connection with food in Visoko. Before the war, I had a friend, a Muslim, his name was Samir Topalovic. His father's name was Fadil, his father was in Kiseljak, he works at the public utilities company, and he received his salary throughout the war. Samir came from Rotilj to see me at the parish house while the roadblock was still there, and he said that he had trouble with his kidneys, and when he went to the toilet that there was blood in his urine, and he asked me whether I could help him get to Visoko and then to Zenica to the hospital. And I did that. When he was supposed to go, he came to see me again, and he asked me whether he would take a parcel of food from Rotilj to Visoko. My friend Samir went and, unfortunately, he got killed in the fighting at Zavrtaljka, and he was brought dead to Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When you say he got killed, what do you mean; later, or then when he was crossing to Visoko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He got killed three months after he left.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You said that in Split you had a warehouse of the Caritas organisation for the entire diocese of Bosnia. Could you tell me who sent supplies to this warehouse and what road you took and what this trip would be like and who you had to discuss this with and how you did it, in general terms. So, please, where was your warehouse, first of all, in Split?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Caritas organisation of the Bosnia diocese got a big warehouse at TTS in order to store their food supplies. Various humanitarian organisations used that warehouse, and the various Caritas organisations of various municipalities, and various Bishop organisations. We got food from many countries, for example, I know for sure from France, Switzerland, Austria, Germany, and particularly Sweden.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Food was in Croatia, and now we have up here on the easel a map where the zones of responsibilities are of the army of Republika Srpska, red colour; green colour, army of Bosnia-Herzegovina; and yellow colour denotes the HVO. Could you explain to the Court which road you had to take and through whose territory and how many kilometres to Split to collect this food?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Do you want me to get up?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, please do, and show this on the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: What is the date of the map? You are defining the zones of influence of the various armies, but it would be better for you to state precisely the month, because the situation would change. You said in blue you have the Bosnian army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: No, no, the Bosnian army is green. Green is the Bosnian army, yellow is the HVO and red is the army of Republika Srpska. During the Washington Accords -- I think it's a mistake, it's a mistake in colours. This is what it looked like after the April conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: There is blue here. The question I'm asking, I should have asked it right away, I don't like to interrupt, but I should have asked this question: If you want to make the explanations of your witness clear, we have to know what is the date that you are defining the places and what the colours represent. If I have understood correctly, the red is the Serbian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: This is the map during the fighting. This is when the Washington Accords were signed, after the war. This is what this map shows. The armies that are shown held this particular area under their control at the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: At the end of the war, then; is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The end of the war, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: So, the red is the Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: And the entire territory indicated in green is what?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Is under control of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: And yellow is what you would call the HVO enclaves; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, that is the territory under HVO control.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: And the blue mark?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The blue should be zones that were under UN control.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So this map is important for us so that we can see who held what territory, so that we could see what the road from Kiseljak to Split was, where humanitarian aid was taken. So Fra Pervan, please show the Court the enclave of Kiseljak, and describe your trip from Kiseljak to Split and back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The enclave of Kiseljak, that is where the tip, this tip here, the tip of the indicator, the pointer. It is, for the most part, surrounded by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. On one short section the enclave of Kiseljak is under the control of the Croatian Defence Council, and this borders on the army of the Republika Srpska. That place is called Kobiljaca, and it is on the road from Kiseljak, Ilidza to Sarajevo. In August we had a lot of refugees already, and there was a threat of catastrophe breaking out. The food supplies had already dwindled and were disappearing, and we were afraid of a catastrophe breaking out. The people responsible in Kiseljak of the civilian military and police authorities there, they contacted the authorities of the Republika Srpska, I think with the approval of their superiors. They decided that from Kiseljak, via the territory of the Republika Srpska controlled by the Serbian army, that a route could be made, a road taken towards Croatia, that is to say, towards Split, which is where we wanted it to go. But that remuneration was to be made, that is, payment was to be made for passing through that way. I started out with a convoy from Kiseljak, and on the small map you can see these places better, and I'm going to enumerate them now. There are quite a lot of these places, but let us take them in this order: Kiseljak, Kobiljaca, Rakovica, Ilidza, Semizovac, Srednje, Vucja Luka, Pale, Han Pijesak, Vlasenica, Zvornik, Bijeljna, Brcko, Samac, Modrica, Doboj, Derventa, Prnjavor, Banja Luka, Prijedor, Glamoc, Bosansko Grahovo, Livno, Tril, Hlis and Split.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How many kilometres is that route in length?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The route is 1.196 kilometres long.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And how far is it from Kiseljak to Split?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Kiseljak, Split is 289 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You may resume your seat. You said that the civilian and military authorities had planned this passage for you to take the humanitarian aid through, they had decided upon that with the Serbs, and you had passed that route several times in another shorter route, as well, and we will mention this later on. Can you describe to us the conditions, the agreement made with the Serbs on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said, that is to say from 1995 up to the present day, I said at least 20 times that if I had to take that route again I would say I'm not going. It was a very difficult route, and a very ugly one. We had MacAdam road surfaces on many occasions, very often we had to have a truck with us, and they would take the food. We were maltreated. We were mistreated both by the Serb soldiers, and there were some words that I cannot repeat to this Court today, and gestures which I cannot show to anybody, they were so, in such poor taste. But we were sworn at, we were cursed, our national identity was cursed and our religion was cursed, in very vulgar terms. And very often we, although we were accompanied by the Serb police, we never reached our destination intact. They took the canvasses off our trucks, and very often there was shooting, and we passed close by to the delineation point between the two armies, the Serb army and the BH army, and the BH army attacked our convoys very often and opened fire on us. In the Posedena region between Orasje and Rijeka, thinking that it was Serb trucks that were passing, the HVO even shot at us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell us, please, whether at one point you were taken hostage for a number of days on Serb territory, and if so, what the conditions accompanying this were.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When the agreement was reached, of course, there was no love lost between us, and it was a very difficult time. At one point we were housed in the camp in Sanski Most, we were put up there, and on another occasion we waited to be given passage, free passage in Stolac up to 11.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Why did they refuse to let you pass?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On one occasion, for 26 hours, I was in prison in Bileca, and what happened was the following: The price of free passage for the convoy carrying food, supplies and clothing was to be paid to the Serbs, and if everything was not okay, the Serbs would wait for the money to be paid in and would hold us hostage during that time. I remember on one occasion the price for passage was ten cisterns of petrol. Ten passed, the tenth was late, and we had to wait until this fuel supply had been met. When I was in Bileca in the prison the conditions were very difficult there. I felt miserable, and I thought that I would never leave that prison. On that occasion, the price was 10.000 Deutschmarks to be paid for free passage. At the entrance to the territory of Republika Srpska this sum was not paid on time and we had to wait in the prison until the money was paid. And they had rifles, which had already been filled with ammunition, so I was afraid of losing my life.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: From your viewpoint, and with regard to the humanitarian convoys, do you think this co-operation was justified?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, as a man, I say that I physically would not have survived this, but in my mind, and in my soul, if necessary, I would justify this tomorrow and I would do it all again, if I were able to go through the same hardships physically. I think that all my sufferings, all the difficulties that I had and my drivers had were nothing compared to how much we were able to save the people, and that was more valuable. The act is always more valuable than the hardships you have to go through to achieve those acts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Court, for us to get a general impression, how big was your convoy? How many tons of food were you able to take in one particular tour of this convoy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the most aid that I was able to take over was 1.032 tons, 44 trucks and one bus, which was full of food, and I gave this food to the Serbian civilians and soldiers; although, we had paid for our free passage, but they wouldn't allow us to pass before we gave them some food. So, at one point I gave them all five tons, and was able to take only ten parcels with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Apart from your convoy, did Kiseljak organise commercial convoys of any kind, in the sense of trade, selling, buying and selling? If so, could you tell us who organised this and the kind of goods that were bought and sold in this way and to whom they were sold?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The municipal authorities, both civilian and military, at that time organised what was known as commercial convoys, and these convoys, too, had to be paid for. I think that they were more expensive than the humanitarian convoys, and thank God they did not bring, they did not bring flour, oil and sugar. For the most part they bought these goods in Croatia and in Europe and then sold those goods.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What goods were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, for example, cigarettes, alcoholic beverage, and goods that were expensive, as well as clothing, footwear, jewellery and watches.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And who were these goods sold to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These goods were sold both in Kiseljak proper; but most of the goods were sold in the area from Kiseljak to Visoko, that is to say, to the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you say, was anything sold to the Serbs, or were any exchanges made with the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was difficult to sell these goods to the Serbs because the Serbs didn't have money to pay for them, and if some of these goods were given to the Serbs, it was on the basis of a barter, of an exchange sort of system.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you consider that this kind of trade, during those war days, on the part of the civilian and military authorities, that a significant amount of money was collected, which represented a certain amount of economic power, which was not typical in other areas as in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. This kind of trade that went on with the Muslim side, and we know today that those goods went up to Tuzla and Zenica, they made Kiseljak economically, and later on, both militarily stronger. For example, Kiseljak had an army, and it was thanks to the goods that it sold in Visoko that it got from the Muslims in Visoko 400.000 pairs of army boots. I know for a fact that from Breza via Visoko, for the primary school and secondary school, we bought coal, and it came from Visoko and Breza, so that our school had heating in the very difficult cold days. Why it had heating, I did not state this, when the refugees came to us and we spoke about the lack of space and that more refugees had to be put up in one house, throughout the war in the primary school and secondary school we had collective lodging for the Croat refugees. This collective housing is ongoing in Kiseljak today, because there are still refugees there, and we still do not have enough flats and houses to accommodate them in.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What about the situation in Kiseljak, as far as supplies were concerned? Were the shops open? Did you have citric fruits and bananas and things that could not have been thought about in Bosnia at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in Kiseljak the shops were open, they worked all the time, as did the cafes. On a regular basis I went to have coffee in the cafes, and a drink, and all the kind of things were functioning which nobody could imagine at that time in the rest of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You personally, did you take part only in the humanitarian convoys, or did you participate in the commercial convoys?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I only took part in the humanitarian convoys. I had nothing to do with the commercial convoys. I knew about them, I knew the prices, I knew what was being sold and the kind of goods they had, but materially speaking, physically speaking, I did not participate in them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: On the map, when you showed us the arrows and the 1.000 kilometre route that you took to Split, there is a shorter route marked with two arrows. Could you explain to the Trial Chamber what that route shows?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the second stage of our travels towards Croatia and Split, we received approval from the Serbs to shorten our route, because they had de-mined a part of their territory around Stolac, so we were able to shorten our route, and that is the route we took later on. That particular route leads from Kiseljak, out of Kiseljak towards Kobiljaca, Rakovica, Ilidza, Semizovac, Srednje, Vucja Luka, Pale, Bukovica, Trnovo, Dobra Polje, and I forgot to mention Foca, and then we have Gacko, we go on to Gacko, and from Gacko up to the cross-roads of Planje, and then on to Berkovici from Berkovici to Stolac, from Stolac to Capljina, from Capljina to Citluk, from Citluk we went to Grude, from Grude to Imovski (phoen) from Imovski, once again, through Senj, or from Capljina we would go down to Metkovic and use the Adriatic road towards Split.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can we, therefore, say that on the map which shows the routes, the route you have just described, leads to the south and is marked with two parallel arrows?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was this map drawn up according to instructions from you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I stuck it together myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Let us move to a different subject now, and that is the way that Kiseljak was cut off from Vitez and Busovaca. When, according to your recollections, were communication lines cut off for the first time between Busovaca and Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to my knowledge, this was in the third decade (sic) of January, the end of January, when conflicts broke out along the edges of the Kiseljak and Busovaca municipality, that is to say, conflicts in Klokoti, as we call this area, it is the village of Bilalova, Klokoti, Kacuni, Gusti Grab, Bukovci, Crpe (phoen), Nezirovci, Besici and Donja Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When you personally were in Busavaca, when were you last in Busovaca and how did you get there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The last time I was in Busovaca was after the conflict in January, that is to say, after the first conflict in Klokoti, a cease-fire reigned and that lasted up until April. As there was a war house in 1992, and I brought food there, I had a war house in my church, I wanted to take food to the Caritas organisation for the parish in Busovaca. One day I went to Bilalovac, I found Mr. Ganu and Mr. Sefer there, they were policemen in Kiseljak, and I knew them, and I asked them to give me permission to take two truckloads of food to Busovaca, and this is what they told me: They said, "We can give you safe passage, and we're going to give it to you, but you have to go to the municipality of Kacuni, and you will receive additional permission there." When they went to Bilalovac they set up the Kiseljak municipality there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Who are you thinking of there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Muslims, the Muslims in Kacuni founded the municipality of Busovaca, and I was given permission by them, and one of their policemen took me to Kacuni, he asked me whether I knew where the house of Enijad Mekic was, Enijad Mekic before the war was a Hodza and he was president of the party of democratic action. I went to his house, I was wearing a uniform, and I found Enijad sitting down wearing a uniform of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When you say you were in uniform, what kind of uniform were you wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, my uniform is the Franciscan, the type of Franciscan robes of our order, that Franciscans all the over the world wear. I said why I had come and we knew each other from before the war, and he took me to Husnija and there was some very unpleasant talks there, but I was given permission. I went back to Kiseljak and on that day in the afternoon I loaded up two trucks and the morning after I left. In Kacuni the trucks were examined in great detail. They didn't curse us, they didn't swear at us, they didn't do anything to us, they let us go towards Busovaca. We unloaded there, went back to Kiseljak, and that was the last time that I went to Kiseljak up until the cease-fire in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You mean the last time you were in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry, Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Would you give us the date? When was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My convoy, you mean? Yes, I think that it was at the beginning of March, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
