utterances.text: When was the territory between Busovaca and Vitez - sorry, Kiseljak, cut off completely? When did you notice this, when was this cut off, and when did you come to the territory, or rather, how did you come to the territory of Kiseljak in May 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the January conflict, when there was a cease-fire, after the Easter holidays, I went through Kresevo, Tarcin and Konjic, and Mostar, I went out of Croatia. I went to Europe. I went on a trip. When I came back from Europe, when I went to Split, I could not reach Kiseljak anymore. I waited for a few days in Split, and then I heard that in Citluk there were also people who wanted to go to Central Bosnia to Kiseljak, Zepce and Vares. I came to Citluk with my own car and my driver, and I asked who wanted to come with me. And I said, "Well, let's go, and let's hope for the best." Many people wanted to come along from Vares, Zepce and Fojnica. In this convoy most of us were Croats, but there were also two Muslims with us, Fuad Curic and Zecevic, I think his name was Osman. We agreed to do this and they were afraid. We agreed to stick together and with the help of God we would finally reach our destination. At 1.00 in the afternoon we went from Citluk to Posusje and then to Duvno, from Duvno over the mountain of Rama. It is a very difficult road. In the evening we arrived in Prozor and we spent the night in front of the Franciscan monastery in Rama near Prozor. In the morning we went to Gornji Vakuf where the cease-fire was still on, and the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the army of the Croatian Defence Council were both there in town. The two of us, my driver and I, and Faud Curic and Zecevic, I think his name as Osman, went to see the local commander of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. We talked to him. We said that we wanted to go home. We asked him to help us, and he made it possible for us to go home. We left Gornji Vakuf, we took the road that leads to Novi Travnik by Sebicic (phoen). We arrived at Sebicic, and then part of this road goes to Fojnica near the Prokosko Lake, and the other road leads to Novi Travnik via Vitez. We went via the lake. When we got to the top of Laska Ravan, behind the trees there were members of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina with their guns aiming at us. And they mistreated us, they cursed at us. Faud Curic and Zecevic went to Fojnica. They were gone for two hours. Then I had to go too. When I got down there by Prokos, a young man pointed his gun at me and put it underneath my neck. He was drunk, and he said, "I'll kill you, because you are from Kiseljak." And then another fellow came by and told this first one not to touch me. We continue our trip. In the evening we arrived in Kiseljak at 10.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What date was this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I arrived on the 7th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, we have to interrupt now and we will resume at 2.45. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The hearing will now resume. Have the accused brought in, please. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: As soon as the witness comes in, let's have Father Ivan brought in. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: If you agree, we can now resume. Mr. Nobilo, take up at the point we left off.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. Pervan, we talked about your return to Kiseljak after the April conflict. That was what we were talking about before the lunch break. Could you tell us what date you entered the Kiseljak municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I entered the Kiseljak municipality on the 7th of May, in the evening hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The 7th of May, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell us, where can you enter the municipality of Kiseljak, at what place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I entered the Kiseljak municipality at Plocari, which means that I took the road leading from Fojnica to Kiseljak. I went that route -- on that route.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was there any danger on the way or on the road entering Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From Fojnica to the entrance to the Kiseljak municipality there were no incidents, but when we came to the village of Luge (phoen), which where the road passes through, we had to stop, and then you have to move right onto a road which isn't an asphalt road, which is an earth -- dirt road, a village road, because we couldn't go up to the Fojnica cross-roads going from Kiseljak to Busovaca, because any movement of men or anything else, and it was night, and we couldn't move without lighting, and there was shooting from Gomionica, strong firing, I think from machine-guns from the direction of Gomionica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And who was at Gomionica in that direction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell the Trial Chamber, please, after returning to Kiseljak, after the conflict at Trajvan (phoen), was there any possibility whatsoever of coming to Busovaca and Vitez, that pocket, the Busovaca-Vitez pocket? Was there a secret road or route that you could reach this area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. There was no route from Kiseljak to Busovaca. Nothing of that kind existed, public or covert, secret. If there was a road, it could only be across Fojnica to the Laska plain, but when we got there the BH army was there, as I said, and the road from Kislejak to Busovaca was cut off from Bilalovac, that is to say from the church in Brestovska, 100 metres away from the church to the lower valley in the municipality of Busovaca. I think this is very simple to explain, that is to say, how the fighting took place between the HVO and the BH army. Every side along its enclave, along the municipality had dug trenches --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Could we shorten this a bit, unless it's very, very important for you, Mr. Nobilo, because, otherwise, we're going to need a lot of time. Excuse me for interrupting here. Of course, you're the one who can see where you're trying to go in terms of your strategy, I'm not trying to force you to do anything, but we're going through a great many details here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, we shall be concluding in 45 minutes' time, but the impossibility of communication between Kislejak and Busovaca, I think, is an important point. But we're not going to use too much of your time on that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Let's leave, for the moment, whether they were asphalt or dirt roads. Could you reach Busovaca to Kiseljak through the fields, or valleys or whatever?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because everything was blocked with two armies on both sides. The roads were blocked and the whole Kiseljak enclave was surrounded by front-lines on both sides, both the BH army and the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The HVO line and then along this line you had the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can we take an example, and we're going to illustrate, by means of that example, that the two Croatian pockets, Kiseljak and Busovaca, operated in different manners. Tell us the price of cigarettes or food, for example, in Kiseljak and what were the prices in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The prices were drastically different. I forgot to take a packet of my own cigarettes, but the price of one packet of cigarettes with 20 cigarettes in Kiseljak was one Deutschmark, In Busovaca that price was 100 Deutschmarks. One litre of oil in Kiseljak was one and a half to two Deutschmarks in Busovaca, 70 Deutschmarks for a friend, 100 for others, and if you knew nobody, it was 200 Deutschmarks. And I believe that you would be able to find people, had they been able to go to Busovaca, they would have invested their 10,000 marks in cigarettes, place them in cigarettes, and earn 1 million marks' profit. But, of course, there was no profit of that kind and people of that kind engaging in anything of that kind. Nobody thought of this because we knew -- everybody knew it was impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell me, in Kiseljak, was there -- were there enough weapons and grenades, and what do you know about the situation in Vitez and Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Kiseljak, as far as I remember, and as far as I heard from the soldiers, had enough ammunition, rifles and mortars, grenades, but later on I heard that in Busovaca there was a shortage of all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you have any explosives?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we did not have explosives. We had to purchase explosives either in Herzegovina or from the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell me, with the friars in Busovaca, how did you communicate with them personally, you yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they sent me, via UNPROFOR, letters and money, and would I answer to their letters, and I would send up to 4 kilograms of coffee and cigarettes via UNPROFOR to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell me, the radio ham station, did you know how to use it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but other people would tune in for me, tune it in for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So did you have frank talks where everybody could take part?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We were linked with all radio hams, amateurs, both in Busovaca, with Belgrade, Zagreb and throughout Europe, anywhere that the radio station could be heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Now, tell me, do you recall any coded messages of the BH army and the man who deciphered those codes? Can you explain to us how this happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, do I remember. Very often I went to the room where the public radio ham station, amateur radio station, was working. Mijo Raso, my friend, was there, Ivica Marjanovic, they were all my friends, and Miss Prgomet. I would have coffee with them, because it was located in the centre of town. They played cards, chess, I listened to messages. There would be 2CC38, that would be the kind of code, and this would be taken to Mijo Raso, and this was deciphered very easily. They were able to decipher what the Muslim soldiers and others -- the messages they sent out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You said that Tihomir Blaskic attended the funeral of Mato Lucic sometime after the 10th of May, because he was killed on the 10th of May. Tell us how he came to the funeral.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was escorted by UNPROFOR in an Armoured Personnel Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was he brought to the cemetery?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. He came to the house where Mato's parents lived, and he used the UNPROFOR APC vehicle, and then he went to Busovaca or Vitez. He went via -- back via Bilalovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: After the funeral of Mato Lucic, that is to say, sometime after the 10th of May, 1993 up to the end of the war in 1994, did you ever see or hear of the fact that Tihomir Blaskic had come to Kiseljak after Mato Lucic's funeral when he was in Kiseljak the last time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Blaskic never, until the cease-fire in 1994, came to Kiseljak. I did not see him nor did I ever hear of him coming.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You said the funeral rites for Colonel Blaskic's father. That was sometime after Mato Lucic's funeral, in the second part of 1993 that is. Tell us, did Blaskic come on that occasion or would he have come had he been able to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Blaskic was not there. I personally buried his father at the Kiseljak cemetery. He did not come on that occasion. Had he been able to, he would have come. I personally believe, I don't want to say anything against Mr. Blaskic, but I think he loved his father more than he loved his mother.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What about the circumstances of the funeral? Was there any shooting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We always had problems with funerals at the Kiseljak cemetery, because on the opposite side from Visoko, which is one and a half kilometres as the crow flies, the cemetery was shelled. That is to say, the grenades fell on the cemetery.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could you now describe to the Court the following: In the course of 1992 you met Colonel Blaskic, and at the beginning of 1993 you met him again. Can you describe him as a man and a soldier? What impression did he leave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I met mister -- Colonel Blaskic in the spring of 1992. I knew that he was appointed as commander of the barracks. We met in the street. He lived in the town itself. We would go and have a drink together, because in -- the war was not ongoing in Kiseljak yet. He went to church, he attended mass and other religious rites, and the impression he left on me, and everybody else, was that he was a quiet man, a serious man, a calm man, an honest man, somebody always who would adhere to his principles. He did not make a lot of noise. He was always calm in presenting his arguments. I think that he was -- did he not like aggression, and I think psychologically and physically he is what I would say a pure man, call a pure man.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: At that time in Bosnia, there were international -- tense international relations. There was tension and antagonisms around the different nations and religions. Can you assess what his attitude was towards members of ethnic groups? Was he an extremist? Was he an extreme nationalist?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time when Mr. Blaskic was in Kiseljak, there were no conflicts between the Muslim and Croat people, and, thereby, the situation was quite different. There was conflict between the army of the Republika Srpska, the Serbs, and the others. I never heard Mr. Blaskic say anything bad about any nationality, or that he would give bad names to other members -- members of other ethnic groups. I never heard him doing anything of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When he came from Kiseljak, he came from Austria where he had fled to from the JNA, and where the parents of his wife had lived for many years and were well-off. Did he explain to you the motives for which from a quiet country like Austria and civilian life, in the spring of 1992 he went to the Kiseljak area? What were his motives for doing so and what were his intentions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We discussed that subject. Mr. Blaskic graduated from the officer school of the Yugoslav People's Army, he was a commander himself in one of the barracks, and he was able to see what was being prepared and what was going on. He was able to see quite clearly that the majority of the cases, 90 per cent of the cases in the army, in the Yugoslav People's army before the war, were that the officers were Serbs. He saw what had happened to Slovenia and Croatia, and he saw what was going to happen to Bosnia-Herzegovina. And so for patriotic reasons he came back, because he knew the Croatian people and the Muslim people do not have enough well-trained, educated and equipped officers. He came back to the region where he used to live, his parents and his sister lived there, his brother who was ill. So he came back from patriotic reasons, patriotic motives, not to get his own back on anybody. He came to help Kiseljak remain where it was and to have Bosnia-Herzegovina remain as it always was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And who at that time was the enemy? Who attacked Bosnia-Herzegovina when he came back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When Mr. Blaskic came to Kiseljak, Bosnia-Herzegovina was being attacked by the army of the Republika Srpska, by the Serbs. It was the Serbs against the Croats and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have talked to -- the indictment. I would like to move to a private session and I will explain the reasons for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. The Judges agree. Perhaps there was an error here on the transcript. Yes, it will be a private session. (Private session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: 2 (redacted) (Open session)

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: In respect of the exhibits, I have no objections, apart from Exhibit 423, which is the very large document on lists of beneficiaries of Caritas. And the only reason I have a reservation is I would like to read it, and it must be, well, I think it's at least 100 pages long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: What objection do you have? Of course, nobody is going to prevent you from reading this voluminous document. You would simply prefer to set a condition for accepting the document on having read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I would like to read it, Mr. President, before accepting it without objection; I suspect there will not be any objection, but I feel foolish accepting a document which I haven't read. The other documents I have no problem with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, that's to your credit, Mr. Cayley, to your credit. All right, you will read the document, and then in the coming days we ask that you not forget to remind us of that, in case my memory fails me.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I will remind you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I won't read it today, I'll read it later on, at the time of our deliberations; so if you don't mind, at the right time you will indicate it to us. Are we now back in a public session? Yes, we are in a public session. All right, the screens have come back up. Mr. Cayley, you will be conducting the cross-examination. Father Pervan, you are going to be asked questions by the Prosecution as part of the cross-examination. If you agree, Father, when you hear the questions, of course, it's normal for you to turn to the Prosecutor, but when you answer, please turn to the Judges. All right? Very well. Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Father, my name is Cayley, these are my colleagues, Mr. Harmon and Mr. Kehoe. I will address you as Mr. Pervan during your cross-examination, I think it makes the transcript clearer, and for the reasons alluded to by the President yesterday. First of all, I would like to talk to you about your role in the charitable organisation, Caritas. Now, you stated that it was in fact your colleagues who regularly entered Rotilj with aid from Caritas and that you were an infrequent visitor; is that correct, to Rotilj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went to Rotilj not all that frequently, but at least once every seven or ten days, and we would hand out the food when there was -- this was perhaps once a month, sometimes more often.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How regularly did your colleagues visit the village of Rotilj, the other Caritas workers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They would go according to need, when needed, and I went privately to have a cup of coffee, and at all other times when I was invited by them to come and visit them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: After the conflict on the 18th of April, 1993, when did you first visit Rotilj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I visited Rotilj when Daniel Furman asked me to bring food from UNPROFOR to the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you give me a date, or an approximate date of that visit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't give you a date now, because I was so excited at the time and they were such difficult times that I don't remember exactly, but I do know that it was during the first cease-fire or lull before the storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So, that would be in April, would it, Father, April of 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't think so, because I came home on the 7th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So, your first visit to Rotilj was in May, or subsequent to the 7th of May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the 7th of May, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And your testimony is that you visited on a regular basis after that, every seven to ten days.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said. And let me add that after the roadblock I went every other day, I went to visit the doctor, the lady doctor, and I discussed the problems she had. So, I would pass the roadblock almost every day, the ramp, as I say, or roadblock.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So now your testimony is that you visited Rotilj after the 7th of May every other day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but I did not talk to the Muslim population, I just passed the roadblock at the beginning; and I talked to them every seven or ten days, and every time that they would come to the office in the parish, and whenever I was invited to go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you require an HVO escort to go into the village of Rotilj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you've provided to the Court very long lists of Caritas beneficiaries which identify the name of the individual and the place in which that beneficiary was located. Do you have any records at all indicating how much aid was supplied to Rotilj and the other Muslim villages during 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The list, Caritas list was jointly kept, the records were jointly kept, because according to our statute and according to my own vocation, my calling, we were not allowed to list people by their ethnic group. So, sometimes we would do it in alphabetical order, and sometimes according to the places, that is to say, the villages they belonged to. I think that in some documents it is stated that my head calculated that each member of Rotilj was given 95 kilograms of food from August '93 to March '94. Furthermore, in the documents, there was a column when the food was issued, and under the column, this was food that I took myself to Rotilj, which was not always recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you have any of those documents with you now indicating how much aid was delivered to the villages in Rotilj, the quantities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I just said, I think that I gave the Defence this document, these documents. We would have to look through them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, the aid that was delivered to Rotilj, how often was there a delivery of humanitarian aid to the village of Rotilj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Humanitarian aid to Rotilj was delivered as I said, every time when food was handed out to everybody. So Rotilj was never an exception when it came to distributing food. There was one case when we gave aid only to the refugees, and only to the Muslims in Rotilj, when the domestic poor were excluded from this handout of food. But whenever aid and relief was given out to the needy, it was always handed out in the village of Rotilj, to everybody, one and all.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you say with some specificity, was it delivered on a monthly basis, or a six-week basis, on an eight-week basis, to the village of Rotilj, aid from Caritas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have a list here of when the food was distributed. In 1993, let us see, it was from the 18th of January to the 22nd of January. In February it was from the 22nd to the 26th. In March it was from the 30th to the 6th of April. In May it was from the 24th to the 31st of May. In June it was from the 7th to the 17th. There was no delivery in August. In September it was from the 6th to the 12th of September. In October there were no deliveries, on the 11th to the 19th of October. And on the 25th of November to the 3rd of December. There was nothing again until February, 1994. So we distributed food when we had it. We were not able to say when we would be distributing the food, it depended on the convoy. I would go and get the food and sometimes I would spend 17 days en route in bringing back the food needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So with, I think, an omission in October, food was delivered on a monthly basis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we should look at the details for each month. If you ask me which particular month you have in mind I will tell you whether food was distributed or not. Ask me a month.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Well, in the break I think it is best if Mr. Nobilo gives me a copy a document, then I can look and we can discuss it, because at the moment we're discussing a document that I can't see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you agree with that, Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, we wanted to speed up proceedings. We have ten kilos of documents, but we haven't brought everything with us now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I knew that in the end it would be my fault, Mr. Nobilo. We'll have to stop. This is as long as we have to go, we have to stop today at five o'clock. Would you like us to take a break right now, Mr. Cayley, so we can look at the document? Otherwise I suggest we take a break in five or six minutes. I'm not making any more decisions today, you make the decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Five or six minutes is fine, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Then take the five or six minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You were aware there were other agencies that were delivering humanitarian aid to Rotilj, indeed to many parts of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that. They did it apart from the parish Caritas organisation, and I acquiesced to this, I knew it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And I think one of those organisations was UNHCR?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And I think, also present in the village of Rotilj, assessing the humanitarian needs of the villages, were UNPROFOR officers and ECMM officials; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think there were the UNPROFOR doctors and many others, and nobody prevented them from helping people, nor could anybody, or did anybody want to prevent this.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you recall the presence of ECMM officials in the village of Rotilj, the European Community Monitoring Mission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wasn't present when they were there, but I know that they were in Kiseljak all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And I think you may have had conversations with them at some stage during 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I talked to the UNPROFOR men and the monitors and everybody else coming from outside, and I did talk to them, then all those talks took place in my house, in my guest room.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you said in your evidence in chief that there was also the Muslim aid foundation, Merhamet; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I remember it well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And you stated that they were also providing humanitarian aid in Kiseljak; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in the course of 1992 until they began to argue amongst themselves. And as long as they had donations from outside, we worked together, and I was very -- and I know Menso Melezovic to this day, and we see each other, he now lives in Fojnica and was the head of the Merhamet, and he came to my house only a few days ago for coffee and a drink.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: When did Merhamet cease to function in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that it could have been at the end of 1992, sometime thereabouts, and it ceased functioning in January when the conflicts broke out between the BH army and the HVO in Klokoti, Kacuni, Bilalovac, those places.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, the Judges in this Court have heard from another witness that the Merhamet warehouse in Kiseljak was plundered and burned down; do you know of that event?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in Kiseljak, and that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And that was done by the HVO in Kiseljak; wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was done by people living in Kiseljak, and they are Croats. I did not see when this actually happened, I did not see them face-to-face. Probably they belonged to the HVO, but they were individuals, they were a group of people, and they did this with the Merhamet warehouse, which is a bad thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We can stop at this point, Mr. President, if you wish, for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will resume at a quarter after 4.00 and work until 5.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We'll now resume have the accused brought in, please. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar as far as the schedule goes, we're very confused. I see that the clock in the courtroom is fast and the ones in the other offices are slow, which makes for all other kinds of problems.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. I have no further comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You are responsible for everything, everything. You have to be responsible for all the clocks, but now we'll give the floor back to Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Pervan, before the break we were discussing the destruction of the warehouse of the Muslim aid foundation Merhamet. Do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I said that the warehouse was destroyed, set fire to and destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you recall when that occurred in 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it occurred at the beginning of the conflict of the BH army and the Croatian Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So would that be January of 1993 or April of 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After April 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, when that warehouse was destroyed, that must have had quite an impact on the Muslim population in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: People were very frightened. That's right; isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you say that individual members of the HVO were responsible for destroying that warehouse. Are you aware as to whether or not there was ever any sort of police investigation into that occurrence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Are you aware of anybody being charged with destroying the warehouse, anybody from the Kiseljak municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you mentioned earlier that you were engaged in running convoys through Bosnia from Croatia to Kiseljak. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I spoke about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How many of those convoys in 1993 did you personally supervise from Croatia to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think at least half of them, but I would have to look at the food distribution and delivery records and then I would know the number of convoys, according to how -- the number of times food was distributed. But from 1992, we counted, up to the end of the war, that 211 times we took food to Kiseljak. Two hundred and eleven times, especially at times when there was no conflicts between the BH army and the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So you would have personally been engaged in roughly a hundred of those convoys, moving food from Croatia to Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About that much, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And how long were you away from Kiseljak during each of these convoy movements? I assume you went from Kiseljak to Croatia, and then from Croatia back to Kiseljak. How long did each convoy take in time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before the conflicts between the BH army and the HVO, those convoys -- we would leave in the morning, early in the morning, and return in the evening. Most of my journeys were between that time. From August 1993, up until the end of the conflict, I went much less because we had fewer convoys. So during that time it could have been -- there could have been 15 convoys during the conflict, and I was in 7 of them, at least 7 of them. The journey was a long one, but later on we would shorten the road and use the route by Stolac, so three days one way. Except the case that I mentioned when the tax had not been paid to the Serbian government and the Serbian army, and on that occasion we stayed 18 days, and that was in August. But otherwise, a maximum of three days. The journey took a maximum of three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So between April of 1993 and January of 1994, how many convoys do you estimate that you supervised from Croatia to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, I think that from August up until April 1994, there could have been a maximum of 15 to 17, and that I supervised half. So at least eight convoys myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And on average, each of those convoys took three or four days, apart from the one where you were imprisoned for a period, I think, and that took 18 days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, 17 days. Ten days and 11 nights, and I spent 26 hours at the prison in Bileca. And I must say to the Court and to you that I was not included in the commercial convoy. So we're only talking about humanitarian convoys, which functioned over a longer period of time, once a month or once every 35 days, whereas commercial convoys would go once a week or twice a week. So I supervised humanitarian convoys alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Father, are you aware, moving on to another subject, are you aware that in July of 1993 the villages of Rotilj reported to the European Community Monitoring Mission that they were almost out of food? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Their report to the Monitoring Mission is something that I'm not aware of, but in July 1993, we did not deliver food to anybody. We had some clothing which we gave out to the refugees who came to Kiseljak, and at the beginning of July, the 2nd, 3rd, and 4th and 5th, refugees from Fojnica arrived, and I know I could not give food out to them either. So we didn't give out food to anyone in the course of that month because we had no food.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you recall personally meeting with representatives of ECMM in August of 1993, where you stated to them that the HVO did not approve of delivery of Caritas aid to Rotilj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall that day and that particular date, but I don't think that that is what I said. Perhaps that was a mistranslation. I could have said, and that was the truth, that certain individuals who wore uniforms, whose sons had died, or brothers had died or had been expelled, that there was resistance on their part as to why I was sending food to the village of Rotilj. I heard criticisms of that kind, but I continued doing what I thought best, and I continued sending food to Rotilj regardless of those criticisms which came from individuals. But never officially, either in written form or orally from the authorities, either military or civilian, were criticisms of that kind or reproaches of that kind made to me, but I know that some people were against giving out food. But we didn't bother about them. We didn't pay attention to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you stated earlier that, in fact, in July of 1993 you didn't supply any aid to Rotilj. In fact, you said you didn't supply aid to anybody, if I'm correct myself; is that correct? You stated that you didn't supply aid to anybody in July of 1993. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not bring convoys. That's what I had in mind when I said that. But we did give out the food that we had. What we had, they were the vestiges of the vestiges. I understood you incorrectly. I thought you were talking about convoys when I did go from Split to Kiseljak so I must understood you, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So what was the availability of supplies in July 1993 to Caritas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Would you clarify your question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you have supplies in Caritas to distribute to the Muslims in Rotilj in July of 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did not have enough food to distribute, but we distributed what food we had. In that month we had mostly clothing and footwear, and nobody needed that because it was exceptionally hot weather at the time, but what we had we handed out.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If I can distribute an exhibit. Unfortunately, it's in English, Mr. Pervan, so you won't be able to read it, but counsel will be able to follow on this exhibit. Mr. Usher. Now, this is a report of the European Community Monitoring Mission, and it's dated the 27th of August of 1993, and I will read to you a relevant paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Counsel, could we have a moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And I'll read to you paragraph 4, which is on page 2 of the document. This is a report by Philippe Sidos and Oscar Meijboom. If it could be placed on the ELMO so the interpreters can follow. "We visited Rotilj where the situation is unchanged. We met the local director of Caritas in Kiseljak, who said that the main problem is the cut of supplies from Split since March. They have the list of Muslims in the Kiseljak area and deliver help for them. They just received an official authorisation from the mayor, 14 August, '93, for that, because it is bad." -- I assume he meant considered bad by some people. Now, Mr. Pervan, is the local director who is referred to in that report, is that you or is that somebody else in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The director is mentioned of Caritas of the collection centre of Kiseljak, and I said before that Kiseljak was the collection centre for bringing in food and from thence it was handed out. The director was Bozo Boric, he is also a clergyman, but it is not me. He is the director of that collection centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, if as Mr. Boric is saying, the mayor of Kiseljak only gave authorisation on the 14th of August, 1993 for the delivery of aid, Caritas aid, how were you able to deliver prior to that date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bozo Boric is a man who worked in Kiseljak, and he is a man -- he is an honest man who very often criticised the authorities for the difficulties that the Muslims were having to undergo. And he wanted to make this official, and he kept writing and saying, "I went to Rotilj." I said that at the beginning. And when UNPROFOR said they could not go because they said it was difficult to go during the night, I did not seek authorisation for that. And that is not the first time that I did not ask authorisation from the municipality, because the -- what I thought was that the church and the State are separate institutions, and that the church has the right to do what it wants. Bozo wanted to legalise all this, and I know he invested a great deal of time and effort to help individual Muslims. I know of one particular family, the family of Aga Ahmic, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, the mayor that is being referred to here is Josip Boro; is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And he's a man you know very well; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, I'll repeat the question again but ask you a preliminary question. Was it possible to take Caritas aid into Rotilj without the authorisation of Josip Boro?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not ask Josip Boro for matters of that kind of.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Why did Father Bozo ask him for authorisation to take aid into Rotilj on the 14th of August, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know any other motive apart from the fact that Bozo was a little unhappy, unhappily disposed towards Josip Boro, not particularly Ivica Rajic, he was not disposed to him. And there were problems at the time with storing the goods that had been delivered, and Bozo Boric wanted to have that in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Josip Boro was the president of the HVO in Kiseljak; wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Josip Boro was the President of the HVO in Kiseljak, but I think that no one asked him about anything. That's what I said when Mr. Nobilo had questioned me at the very end of his questioning. I explained that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So what you're saying is that this official authorisation by Josip Boro to take aid into Rotilj was meaningless?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that that authorisation was received at a meeting of the civilian and military authorities, and then Josip Boro signed it. That is my opinion. At that time not a single deal of significance was reached without this kind of a meeting between Josip Boro as the head of the municipality, Ivica Rajic as head of the military, and Vinko Antunovic. And I don't know who else was there because I never attended these meetings, but Josip Boro signed all these documents as head of the HVO because that was the set-up then.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So this authorisation would have been approved by the HVO military authorities; is that what you're saying to the Judges?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that both the military and civilian authorities had to authorise this together. That's what I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I will ask you one last time, Mr. Pervan. How was it possible to take aid into Rotilj, prior to the 14th of August, without authority from the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could do that because I did not ask. I did not ask for permission until the present day for humanitarian assistance and aid, who I would give something to. I did not allow any of the military or any of the municipality people to come to the warehouse of Caritas and to see what was there. Never, from the very beginning until the present day, did I allow the municipality, the military or the police to have insight into who things were distributed to, how much and when.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So why did Father Bozo request authorisation to take aid into Rotilj?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have been repeating the same question for a few times now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Legally speaking, Bozo Boric received authority for this, but it was wrong for him to ask for this permission, and it was wrong to then get authority for it, because the village of Rotilj did not belong to his scope of work, because he was head of the collection centre, and it was the municipal Caritas that was supposed to handle this affair. I know Bozo. He's a man who likes to write, he's an honest man, but he did things in a different way. So that is my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Father, you both worked for the same organisation in the same town.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The same organisation and the same collection centre, but this was by accident that this collection centre was in Kiseljak. We worked, but Bozo Boric was only the director of that collection centre, he was not in charge of a single parish in Kiseljak. So he was not my superior in any way. And if this kind of permission was to be sought, I was the one who was supposed to seek it, and I did not think that I should seek permission from anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned a moment ago that Bozo Boric -- I'm sorry if I'm not saying his name correctly -- voiced a number of criticisms in respect to the HVO authorities in Kiseljak. What were those criticisms that he voiced?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Such criticisms were certainly voiced in terms of what happened to Merhamet, what happened to other houses, what happened to people, and by virtue of my own vocation, I spoke about this from the alter too, and I told people about this for several weeks, that is to say, every Sunday when they came to mass. I have documents to prove that, and I can show them to you over here. So this is criticism against destruction, against torching, against killing, against looting, and that is the kind of criticism that I voiced every Sunday and I can show it to you right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And this was in respect of torching Muslim homes, killing Muslim people; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Our criticism pertained to soldiers, individuals from the HVO who did evil in our parish, primarily towards Muslims but also towards other people, especially refugees belonging to the same ethnic group.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And what did the HVO authorities in Kiseljak do after these complaints were made about this conduct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not write to the HVO in Kiseljak. I voiced this criticism in public, from the alter, in front of people, because I thought, and I still think today, it is better to speak to those people who did that. And I know that Ivica Rajic and Bozo Boric, did not order this. I spoke to the parents, and brothers and sisters of those people who did this, that this was evil and they were not supposed to loot, that they were not supposed to kill, that they were not supposed to hoard wealth in an unfair way. So that is why I told them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did Father Bozic make representations to the HVO in Kiseljak about the looting and the torching of Muslim homes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, are you aware that during 1993 Muslim women from Rotilj would come to the Caritas warehouse with permission to collect aid? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You never heard any accounts of Muslim women being beaten in the town on their way to the Caritas warehouse? Did you ever hear about that, Mr. Pervan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, I wish to say something else. When these women -- these Muslim women came to see me in my office at the church, they never asked for permission, nor did they ever show me anything of the kind. I did hear about this kind of excessive behaviour in Kiseljak. It is not only women that were attacked but Muslim men too.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We'll come to permission from the HVO later in your cross-examination, but can you tell the court what you heard about people being beaten in the town on their way to the Caritas warehouse?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard that there were such cases, that Muslims, men or women, as they were going to Kiseljak to buy something, that they had some bad things happen to them, that some were even beaten. And, Your Honours, I condemned this from the alter and I can show you here what I spoke of then.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the next exhibit, Mr. Usher, could be distributed. While that's being distributed, Mr. Pervan -- I'm sorry. Please --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is 541, 541A for the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: This was the HVO authorities who were your landlord in Kiseljak, they provided Caritas with accommodation. That's correct; isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you look at the document that's in front of you now, it's a document signed by Josip Boro, who was the president of the HVO, and confirm that this is the document which authorised Caritas to occupy certain premises in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as this document is concerned, I am aware of it, Your Honour. This is the document that Josip Boro issued to Fra Bozo Boric, and this is where he worked, he and his secretary, and this document is not related to Caritas of the Kiseljak parish.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: To which Caritas does this document relate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This relates to the collection centre in Kiseljak, number 1. That was the name of this collection centre. And Father Bozo Boric represented it on behalf of the Verbonsiska diocese. So this was a collection centre for all the parishes. The other one was in Split. And even today there is such a collection centre in Tuzla, in every diocese. And in this document a mistake was made by the President of the municipality. This is related only to this office where Father Bozo and his secretary were. Fra Bozo and his secretary have nothing to do whatsoever with the Caritas of the parish of Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So there were two Caritas in Kiseljak; is that what you're saying to the Judges?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the municipality of Kiseljak there were four Caritas. The Caritas of Ban Brdo, the Caritas of Kiseljak parish, of the Grominyak parish and of the Brestosko parish, all of them took goods from this joint collection centre. When Fra Bozo stopped going there, because he did not want to go through Serb territory, and I brought this food in then, and then he gave the supplies to the Caritas in all the parishes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is going too fast for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And this is what we did through this collection centre. He was only director of this centre, but Bozo had nothing to do whatsoever with the distribution of the food. And as director of the collection centre, he could give food to individual persons or individual members.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Pervan, could you speak a little more slowly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. Try to speak a little more slowly. You understood what my colleague wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So I'm not fully clear on the position in respect of this document. Am I right in saying that these premises were a collection point where all of the various Caritas in Kiseljak would collect goods from this accommodation referred to in the document, and then it would be distributed on from there? Is that the position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that is not the way things are, and I shall try to explain once again. The premises that Fra Bozo got is a room of 20 square metres, 4 by 5 metres. So it is an office really. And Fra Bozo got this on the 25th of February, 1993. That is to say, when there was a cease-fire that was still on, there was no fighting between the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the Croatian Defence Council, Bozo wanted to bring these goods in. However, then the war broke out, and then Bozo would come to this room every now and then when we would bring in this food. He lived in the parish of Lepenica. That's where he was the priest. And this was a small room that served as an office. There were four chairs, a desk, and a typewriter and a very small coffee set.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pervan. In your conversations with the local people in Rotilj, did they tell you that the livestock in the village had either been killed in April or had been subsequently stolen from them? Did they tell you that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges what you know about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When the conflict broke out at Rotilj I was not in Kiseljak, I heard about these conflicts, I heard about the dead, and I heard that there were some houses that were on fire. I heard that some of them were ablaze because the hay went on fire, and I heard that some of the livestock was killed. But I wasn't there. That's what I heard. When I came back to Kiseljak in May, in Rotilj the fighting, the conflict was over, and there was no fighting anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm now going to proceed to another area, so, it may be a good time to finish for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. Let me remind you that as regards tomorrow, we will be sitting in the morning from 10.00 to 1.00, tomorrow afternoon it will start at 2.30, and we will stop at about five minutes or ten minutes to 5.00, I don't know exactly, I have to get the details, because the Judges have been asked to come to a meeting in honour of a visit by a person to the International Criminal Tribunal. Let me remind you that Thursday there is no morning session, but we will begin at 3.00, and Friday we will proceed as usual, whereas, the following week there are no hearings at all. Court stands adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: 4.58 p.m., to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 4th day of November, 1998 at 10.00 a.m.
